briefing.text: The hypothesis is about microsatellite-stable tumors, but the tables have no MSI column. MSI/MMR-deficient and POLE-mutant tumors have extreme TMB, MMR signatures (SBS6/15/20/21/26/44, ID1/ID2) or POLE signatures (SBS10a/b), and strong ICB responses, so they can drive any signature-response association. Flag hypermutators (TMB far above the cohort distribution), samples with a high MMR-signature fraction or indel-heavy profiles, and samples with MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2/POLE mutations. Exclude them and re-run.
briefing.reason: Without this the team may test a cohort that includes MSI/POLE tumors, which is not the population the claim is about and can produce a spurious association.

briefing.text: The patient table has several response definitions (RECIST_RESPONSE, RECIST, VA_RESPONSE, ROH_RESPONSE as clinical benefit vs no clinical benefit) plus PFS/OS. How stable disease is handled can change the result. Cross-tabulate the definitions and count missing or intermediate values. Choose one binary endpoint as primary before testing and report the others as sensitivity analyses. Drop missing or intermediate values instead of coding them as non-response.
briefing.reason: The choice of endpoint and the coding of SD can flip the signature-response association, so the endpoint has to be fixed before looking at results.

briefing.text: Signatures such as UV (SBS7) and smoking (SBS4) add mutations, so a signature-response link can work through TMB. Report both the marginal association and the association after adjusting for log TMB (TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS or SNV count), and keep absolute counts (which track TMB) apart from relative fractions. Background knowledge, not web-verified and of low-to-medium confidence: ICB genomics papers usually report signature-response links as marginal associations and treat TMB as a mediator on the causal path, not a confounder. Under that convention the marginal test is the test of the claim, and the adjusted model shows whether the effect works only through TMB.
briefing.reason: Whether the deciding test is marginal or TMB-adjusted can change the label. The team needs both results and the reporting convention to choose between them.

briefing.text: In a pan-cancer ICB cohort, signatures track cancer type (SBS7 UV = melanoma, SBS4 smoking = lung, SBS2/13 APOBEC = bladder and head-neck), and response rates also differ by cancer type. Tabulate CANCER_TYPE against response and against each signature's exposure. Then adjust for cancer type (stratified test or logistic regression) and/or test within melanoma and NSCLC separately.
briefing.reason: Cancer-type mix can create or hide a signature-response association, which changes how the pooled result should be read.

briefing.text: Testing many signatures across many cancer-type subgroups produces false positives. Count the signature-by-subgroup tests, apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, and report q-values for every signature-response association. Give the pre-specified pan-cohort test the most weight.
briefing.reason: A single nominal p of about 0.05 among many tests should not decide the label.

briefing.text: Derive signatures from data_mutations.txt using one tumor sample per PATIENT_ID. Include all SNVs, silent ones too, with Variant_Type == SNP, and leave DNPs and indels out of SBS-96. Check that the build is GRCh37. Count SNVs per sample: refitting is unreliable at low counts (well under about 20-50 SNVs). If counts are low, refit only the dominant signatures (SBS1, SBS2/13, SBS4, SBS5, SBS7, MMR) or compare simple spectra such as the C>A fraction, the C>T-at-dipyrimidine fraction and the TCW fraction.
briefing.reason: Signature estimates that overfit or count patients twice would undermine any association test.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume four hand-picked trinucleotide-context proxies (UV, tobacco, APOBEC, clock CpG) capture the 'global mutational signatures' of the hypothesis; neither tested other processes (e.g. MMR/POLE, alkylating, unknown) or a fitted decomposition.

Both treat each sample's SNV fractions as independent of TMB and cancer type in the primary (marginal) test, while both found the signal attenuates after TMB/cancer-type adjustment; the choice of marginal test as primary decided the label.
Both assume all 249 samples are in scope as 'microsatellite-stable' although there is no MSI column; hypermutator exclusion was a sensitivity analysis only.
Both assume every mutation row counts equally (all variant classes, no filter on germline probability or read support).
unused_evidence: Clonality columns in the mutation table (ccf_hat, clonal_dm, Pr_somatic_clonal, Pr_subclonal) were not used; signatures could be computed on clonal vs subclonal mutations, which may change which signatures associate.
Pr_germline, t_alt_count/t_ref_count and n_alt_count were not used to filter low-confidence or germline calls, which affects context fractions in low-SNV samples.
PFS/OS survival columns, DRUG_TYPE, OTHER_CONCURRENT_THERAPY and SMOKING_PACK_YEARS were not used; smoking history could validate the tobacco proxy and drug type is a possible confounder.
The CNA segment file was not used (it bears on purity/aneuploidy, not directly on signatures).
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named 'simple context proxies, not fitted decomposition' as weakest point and neither resolved it.
Both named attenuation after TMB adjustment and resolved it only by declaring marginal tests primary, not by testing within tumour type or with TMB-matched comparison.
Team B named melanoma dominance entangling UV with tumour type; within-melanoma UV test (team A) was reported only briefly.
second_readings: 'Associated with response' could mean marginal association (the teams' reading) or an association independent of TMB/tumour type; the label may hinge on which reading the source study used.
'Global' signatures could mean genome-wide SNV-spectrum processes across all tumour types pooled, versus signatures within each cancer type.
'Response' could be RECIST objective response, clinical benefit (VA/ROH) or survival; the teams used three binary endpoints but not PFS/OS.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust: both teams found clear marginal signature-response associations with FDR control across endpoints, and robustness to hypermutator exclusion, but the signal attenuates after TMB/cancer-type adjustment and both used crude proxies, so the label rests on the marginal reading of 'associated'.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your clock-CpG and APOBEC signals lose significance after TMB and cancer-type adjustment. Within melanoma and within NSCLC separately, do responders and non-responders differ in each signature fraction when stratified by TMB tertile? Does that result change whether the marginal test should decide the label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Did you check that the tobacco proxy tracks SMOKING_PACK_YEARS/SMOKER and the UV proxy tracks melanoma histology? If a proxy does not track its exposure, does that change which signatures you can test?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: How do signature fractions change if you drop calls with high Pr_germline or low t_alt_count, and if you compute them on clonal mutations only (clonal_dm/ccf_hat)? Does any association appear or disappear?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You checked four signatures. Did you test any other spectrum features, e.g. an MMR/POLE-like or C>A-dominant fraction, or a full 96-channel comparison between responders and non-responders? Would a broader screen with FDR change the conclusion?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You treat TMB as a mediator. Do the signature associations hold within single tumour types (melanoma, NSCLC) and after stratifying by TMB tertile? Does that result change whether the marginal test should decide the label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Did you check that the smoking proxy correlates with SMOKING_PACK_YEARS/SMOKER and that DRUG_TYPE or OTHER_CONCURRENT_THERAPY are not unbalanced across responders? Does adjusting for drug type change the results?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: How do the signature fractions and their association with response change if you filter calls by Pr_germline and read support (t_alt_count, n_alt_count), or restrict to clonal mutations (clonal_dm/ccf_hat)?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Do the signature associations replicate with PFS (PFS_MONTHS/PFS_STATUS) or OS in a Cox model? If the survival result disagrees with the binary endpoints, does that change your label?

questions.why: Both teams used context proxies instead of fitted signatures and named this as their weakest point.

findings.question: In pan-cancer immune checkpoint blockade genomic cohort studies, when a mutational signature is reported as associated with response, is the association usually tested marginally or after adjustment for tumour mutational burden and tumour type?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on all 3 calls, so no page was read. From background knowledge: these studies (e.g. the Miao et al. 2018 pooled WES ICB cohort) usually report the association first as a marginal test (Mann-Whitney or univariate logistic regression), and the headline finding rests on that. Adjustment for TMB and tumour type is a secondary check. Smoking and UV signatures are generally expected to weaken after TMB adjustment because they act through TMB, which is treated as a mediator rather than a confounder. So a marginal association that weakens after adjustment would still typically be reported as 'associated with response'.

findings.question: How well do simple trinucleotide-context fractions (e.g. C>T at CpG, CC>TT/C>T at dipyrimidines, C>A, TCW>T/G) agree with COSMIC SBS exposures fitted by deconstructSigs or SigProfiler in whole-exome data?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the gateway returned HTTP 403. From background knowledge: agreement is good for signatures with sharp, distinctive patterns: UV/SBS7 (C>T at dipyrimidines; CC>TT is very specific), APOBEC/SBS2+13 (TCW>T/G; the Roberts et al. APOBEC enrichment score is a standard proxy), and smoking/SBS4 (C>A). It is weaker for SBS1 (C>T at CpG), which in exome data is inflated by GC-rich exons and overlaps the MMR/POLE signatures. It is poor for flat signatures (SBS3/5/40). Fitted exposures are themselves unreliable in WES samples with fewer than about 50 mutations (the deconstructSigs guidance), so for low-TMB samples a proxy is about as reliable as a fit. Proxies are adequate for the dominant UV, APOBEC and smoking signals, but not for exact exposures.
